title: Repeated exposure can make a new thing more likeable
body: A 2017 review combined experiments on the mere exposure effect. On average people tended to like things more after seeing them again, though the gains did not keep rising without limit.
takeaway: Give an unfamiliar song a few listens before deciding whether your first impression holds up.
visual: a hand returning a plain record to a turntable

title: Decorative animations hurt recall in one learning experiment
body: In a study published in 2020, students viewed lessons with or without decorative animations or still pictures. Participants presented with the decorative animations recalled less of the instructional content.
takeaway: When making slides, let any movement point to the thing you want people to notice.
source: Decorative Animations Impair Recall, Advances in Physiology Education (2020)
visual: a person watching a simple presentation with a small distracting moving shape at the edge

title: A change of schedule can create jet lag without travel
body: In 2006 Marc Wittmann and colleagues used sleep surveys to compare people's sleep timing on work days and free days. They called the difference in the middle of a person's sleep periods social jet lag.
takeaway: You can measure the change by comparing the midpoint of sleep on two kinds of day.
visual: two bedside clocks sitting on opposite sides of a window blind

title: One participant trained from remembering seven digits to 79
body: In a study published in 1980, one participant practised repeating sequences of digits for more than 230 hours. He increased his span from seven digits to 79 by organising the digits into meaningful groups.
takeaway: The gain came from a way of organising information, so it need not transfer to unrelated things you try to remember.
visual: a line of small wooden beads separated into clusters on a desk
